newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bonds close higher on inflation outlook.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bonds close higher on inflation outlook.

text.p: Israeli bonds closed higher across the board on Monday on continued expectations of declining inflation in 1997, traders said.
* Unlinked government bonds (Gilon -- issued for four years): +0.11 pct to 172.23
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.04 pct to 162.14
Volume was moderate at 185 million shekels with most activity concentrated in unlinked bonds.
"The market rose today because investors are predicting that inflation will continue to decline in the next few months," said one trader.

He said inflation-linked long bonds rose while short- and medium-term bonds declined as investors moved to unlinked bonds. "They are predicting that the Bank of Israel will soon lower its key lending rate," he said.
Traders noted that the Bank of Israel is expected to lower the base rate, now 15.2 percent, by at least one percentage point after parliament approves the 1997 budget. The deadline is December 31.
After the close of trading, the cabinet approved a further 1.2 billion shekel budget cut on top of the 4.9 billion shekels of cutbacks included in the original 1997 budget of 190.8 billion shekels.

"Prices for unlinked bonds continue to rise despite declining yields. The market is waiting for a relatively low December CPI (consumer price index) of around 0.5 percent," said Ari Eidelheit at Zeller Eblagon Securities.
"Investors predict that 1997 inflation will be around 8-9 percent," he said, noting that yields on the Makams, which are also unlinked, fell to only 14.2 percent.
"Yields on the Makams are extremely low. I belive that in the near future we will see a correction and yields will rise," the other trader said.

Dollar-linked bonds rose following the rise of the dollar against the shekel. In the local foreign currency market on Monday the representative rate for the dollar was fixed at 3.2820 shekels against 3.2730 on Friday.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
